did_you_know.text: Did you know? Babylon is described as a “golden cup” in the Lord’s hand because many nations drank her wine, became drunk, and boasted; the image expresses Babylon’s corrupting influence on the nations.

Did you know? In contrast to Babylon’s idols, the chapter presents the Lord as the one who made the earth by his power, established the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding.
Did you know? Babylon is called a “war club” and a weapon in the Lord’s hand; through her, nations, kingdoms, horses, chariots, and leaders are described as being struck down.
Did you know? In the prophecy, nations and kingdoms are called to gather against Babylon, including Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, along with the kings of Media and all the land under their rule.
Did you know? Babylon’s fall is portrayed through messengers running to meet one another to announce to the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end.
Did you know? Jerusalem describes Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as one who swallowed and emptied her, and she declares that the violence and bloodshed inflicted on her will be charged to Babylon.

Did you know? The Lord declares that he will punish Bel, the Babylonian deity, and take from his mouth what he has swallowed; nations will no longer stream to him. The same verse also says that Babylon’s wall has fallen.
Did you know? In the midst of the prophecy of destruction comes a direct call to the Lord’s people: “Come out of her, my people”—flee from Babylon because of the Lord’s fierce anger.
Did you know? Babylon’s broad walls and high gates are destined to be shaken and burned, and those who labor to build her are described as having worked in vain.

Did you know? Jeremiah delivered the prophecy about Babylon to Seraiah son of Neriah, who went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of Zedekiah’s reign; Seraiah is described as the “chief officer of rest.”

Did you know? Jeremiah instructed them to tie a stone to the scroll of the prophecy and throw it into the Euphrates, symbolizing Babylon’s sinking and her inability to rise again because of the disaster that would come upon her.
